activity.title: "You're too privileged to play it safe." The co-founder of a billion dollar company said that at a talk, and it really stuck with me. At the end of the day, I'm surrounded by people who grew up in a home and food on their plate. I feel like if you're that privileged, when there are people out there wondering where their next meal is coming from, you almost have an obligation to go take risks. Make something that changes the world. And because you are in a position to do so, to not is almost a waste. My parents worked their asses off to get me where I am today. Obviously nothing is forcing me to work my ass off, but they worked this hard for me, so I might as well take advantage of it. Mostly I just feel lucky to be in the position to even think about it this way. If you agree/disagree, let me know what your thoughts are. ...more

K factor is probably the most misunderstood metric in startup growth most founders treat it like a binary. either your viral coefficient is above 1 and you scale exponentially, or it's below 1 and you're just lighting money on fire with paid acquisition. that's a myth. sustained K > 1 is rare. for 95% of startups the real value is in viral amplification. think of K as a discount on your CAC. acquire 100 users through ads or SEO with a K of 0.3 and those users bring in 30 more for free. those 30 bring 9. and so on. your 100 becomes 143. that's a 43% lift on your marketing spend for pretty much free also velocity matters more than volume. a K of 0.8 where people invite within 48 hours beats a K of 0.9 where it takes a month. how fast the loop closes is what makes the curve bend. and without retention K is meaningless. high virality plus low retention just means you're burning through your TAM faster. stop wasting energy chasing a mythical K > 1. ...more

"confident people walk around CERTAIN they'll win." That's the picture most of us have But nobody actually knows that they'll win. I used to think I was ambitious, then I came to San Francisco. I met people who genuinely believed they were going to change how an entire industry works, and meant it. These were people betting years of their lives on ideas that, by any reasonable measure, probably wouldn't work. And they talked about it like it was already done. It was contagious. You sit across from someone who casually assumes they'll win, and your own sense of what's possible changes. I didn't get more talented by being around them. My baseline for what's "normal" moved. This is the most underrated reason to put yourself in rooms you don't fully belong in yet. Spend enough time around people who refuse to be realistic and you slowly stop being so realistic yourself :) Photo: Golden Gate Bridge with Friends ...more

Imposter syndrome runs on one assumption: that somewhere there's a version of you who actually belongs in the seat you're in. And you're the fake sitting in for them. But that person doesn't exist. You're the only version of you there is. There's nobody to be an imposter of. You can't be a fake of yourself. So why do you feel it? Two reasons. Both (in my opinion) are good things. 1. everyone around you is genuinely ahead of you. That's a great room to be in. You should always want to be the one with the most to learn. If you're never the least experienced person at the table, you picked the wrong table. 2. the room is at a normal level, and you're just behind it. Even this works in your favor Because being aware of your shortcomings is a genuine advantage that you have. The first step to solving a problem is to understand it! Anyway, that's my sober thought for today. Photo: group of talented individuals (except me 😆 ) ...more

At Uber, shipping software was a coordination problem. Design had Figma. Engineering had code. Product had a roadmap. None of them described the same reality. Teams spent hours in meetings reconstructing what had shipped, what had changed, and what still needed work. That was difficult when humans made every change. Now coding agents produce work an order of magnitude faster then humans. The old coordination layer cannot keep up. So we built Revyl to give people and agents the same view of reality. What once required days of meetings and manual work now happens asynchronously in the clooud. Software is becoming autonomous. The infrastructure around it needs to do the same.

Turns out 3 weeks in SF is a lot of life. met people i’d wanted to meet for over a year and said yes to things my past self would’ve normally overthought i think a past version of me would’ve cared a lot about getting to do all of this. being in sf, meeting certain people, going certain places. and it is still cool but when you’re actually living it, none of it feels like some big milestone. it’s just a moment you happen to be in i think the number one thing holding me back for a long time was thinking in a time that didn’t exist we think about the past because it’s comfortable. we use what happened before as evidence for what we should or shouldn’t do now. then we think about the future and convince ourselves there’ll be a better time to try something, say something, go somewhere but the past isn’t here anymore, and the future has never happened there’s a difference between being strategic about your life and thinking about it so much that you forget to actually live it. i’ve been reassured for awhile now that a lot of the best decisions never came from having every variable figured out maybe being present is just learning not to leave a moment before it’s over because eventually the labels, titles and accolades get forgotten anyway the stories stay the random nights, the people you met, the things you tried, the times you went for it when you could’ve simply not done it. those are the things you actually get to keep it was a pleasure sf. see you soon :)
